articles.title: Fixing For Loops in Go 1.22
articles.author: Russ Cox
articles.text:
Go 1.22 gives each iteration of a for loop its own copy of the loop variable, so closures and goroutines started in the loop no longer share one variable by accident.

The old behaviour caused real bugs: a goroutine or a closure captured the loop variable and saw its last value instead of the value of its own iteration. Go 1.21 offers a preview behind GOEXPERIMENT=loopvar, and the change only applies to modules that declare Go 1.22 or later in their go.mod, so old code keeps its meaning. The Go toolchain ships a tool to find the loops whose behaviour changes.

articles.title: Profile-guided optimization in Go 1.21
articles.author: Michael Pratt
articles.text:
Profile-guided optimization is ready for production in Go 1.21.

Put a CPU profile collected in production in the main package as default.pgo, and the compiler uses it to inline the hot calls more aggressively and to devirtualise interface calls on the hot path. Typical programs get a few percent faster with no change to their code. The Go toolchain builds with the profile by default, and a profile from an older version of the code still helps, so the profile does not need to be collected again for every release.

articles.title: Structured Logging with slog
articles.author: Jonathan Amsterdam
articles.text:
Go 1.21 adds log/slog to the standard library: structured logs as a message, a level, and key-value pairs.

A handler writes each record as text or JSON, and handlers can be swapped or wrapped to filter, enrich, or send records elsewhere. Attributes can be grouped, and the API is designed to be fast enough for hot paths, with few allocations. Before slog, every project chose its own structured logging package; the standard library now gives them a common interface.

articles.title: Go 1.22 is released!
articles.author: Eli Bendersky, on behalf of the Go team
articles.text:
Go 1.22 brings a per-iteration loop variable, which fixes a long-standing source of bugs with closures and goroutines, and range over integers.

The standard library gains enhanced routing patterns in net/http, with methods and wildcards in ServeMux patterns, and a new math/rand/v2 package. The runtime lowers the memory overhead of the garbage collector and improves CPU performance, and the compiler makes better use of profile-guided optimization, with more devirtualisation and inlining.

articles.title: Routing Enhancements for Go 1.22
articles.author: Jonathan Amsterdam, on behalf of the Go team
articles.text:
In Go 1.22 the ServeMux of the standard library net/http package accepts patterns with an HTTP method and wildcards, such as GET /items/{id}.

A handler reads a wildcard with Request.PathValue. When two patterns overlap, the more specific one wins, and conflicting registrations panic. Many small web services can now do their routing with the standard library alone, without a third-party router.

articles.title: Range Over Function Types
articles.author: Ian Lance Taylor
articles.text:
Go 1.23 lets a for loop range over function types: an iterator is a function that calls yield for each element.

The standard library adds the iter package with the Seq and Seq2 types, and new functions in the slices and maps packages return iterators. User-defined containers can now be used in a for range loop like the built-in slices and maps, and the compiler inlines simple iterators so they cost little.

articles.title: Govulncheck v1.0.0 is released!
articles.author: Julie Qiu, for the Go security team
articles.text:
Govulncheck reports the known vulnerabilities that affect a Go project, from the Go vulnerability database.

It analyses the call graph, so it reports only the vulnerabilities in functions the code actually calls, which keeps the noise low. It runs on the command line, in editors through gopls, and in continuous integration with a GitHub Action. The Go vulnerability database is curated by the Go security team and fed by public advisories, which helps against software supply chain risk.

articles.title: How Go Mitigates Supply Chain Attacks
articles.author: Filippo Valsorda
articles.text:
Go modules were designed with the software supply chain in mind.

The go.sum file and the checksum database make every build fetch exactly the code that was reviewed, the module proxy keeps versions available even when their source disappears, and building code does not run code from dependencies. Versions are locked until the developer upgrades on purpose, and the culture of a large standard library keeps the number of dependencies small. None of this removes supply chain risk, but it narrows the attacks that work.

articles.title: Announcing Rust 1.82.0
articles.author: The Rust Release Team
articles.text:
Rust 1.82 adds cargo info to describe a package from the registry, and precise capturing with use<..> bounds on impl Trait.

It also brings a native syntax for raw pointers with &raw const and &raw mut, and safe items inside unsafe extern blocks, which makes the boundary of unsafe code more precise. The compiler and the standard library gain many smaller fixes.

articles.title: Announcing Rust 1.75.0
articles.author: The Rust Release Team
articles.text:
Rust 1.75 stabilises async fn and return-position impl Trait in traits, a long-awaited step for asynchronous code.

A trait can now declare async methods directly, without boxing every future or relying on a macro. The release also brings pointer byte offset APIs, and the compiler itself was built with code layout optimisations that make it faster.

articles.title: Announcing Rust 1.85.0 and Rust 2024
articles.author: The Rust Release Team
articles.text:
Rust 1.85 stabilises the Rust 2024 edition, the largest edition so far, and async closures.

The edition changes the language in ways that would break old code, so each crate opts in, and cargo fix migrates most code automatically. Among the changes, extern blocks must be marked unsafe, and more operations require an explicit unsafe block, which makes unsafe code easier to audit. Crates on different editions keep working together.

articles.title: Eliminating Memory Safety Vulnerabilities at the Source
articles.author: Jeff Vander Stoep and Alex Rebert
articles.text:
Android reports that memory safety vulnerabilities fell from about three quarters of its vulnerabilities in 2019 to about a quarter in 2024.

The main reason is Safe Coding: writing new code in memory-safe languages such as Rust and Kotlin, rather than rewriting old C and C++ code. Vulnerabilities are concentrated in new code and decay as code ages, so changing how new code is written pays off quickly. Memory-safe languages remove whole classes of vulnerability, and interoperability lets them grow inside an existing code base.

articles.title: The Case for Memory Safe Roadmaps
articles.author: CISA, NSA, FBI, and international partners
articles.text:
Government security agencies ask software manufacturers to publish memory safety roadmaps.

Memory safety vulnerabilities, such as buffer overflows and use after free, remain among the most common and severe vulnerabilities in software written in C and C++. The guide recommends memory-safe languages such as Rust, Go, Java, C#, and Swift for new code, and a plan for the existing code: which components to move first, how to train developers, and how to report progress. It is part of the secure by design effort.

articles.title: Rust in the Linux kernel
articles.author: The Linux kernel documentation
articles.text:
The Linux kernel documentation explains how to write kernel code in Rust.

Rust support lets drivers and other modules be written in a memory-safe language, while unsafe code stays confined to the abstractions that wrap the C interfaces of the kernel. The pages cover the build requirements, the coding guidelines, and the general information on how safe Rust abstractions are designed, so that a driver written in safe Rust cannot cause memory safety bugs in the rest of the kernel.

articles.title: Concurrency control: an introduction to MVCC
articles.author: The PostgreSQL Global Development Group
articles.text:
PostgreSQL keeps data consistent with multiversion concurrency control: each statement sees a snapshot of the data as it was some time ago, whatever other transactions are doing.

Reading never blocks writing and writing never blocks reading, which is why the database scales well under concurrent load. The price of MVCC is that an update leaves the old row version behind as a dead tuple, which vacuum must later reclaim.

articles.title: Using EXPLAIN
articles.author: The PostgreSQL Global Development Group
articles.text:
EXPLAIN shows the plan the query planner chose for a statement: the scans, joins, and sorts, with estimated costs and row counts.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE also runs the query and reports actual times and rows, so wrong estimates, a missing index, and slow nodes become visible. The query planner relies on table statistics, which ANALYZE and autovacuum keep up to date; stale statistics are a common cause of a bad plan.

articles.title: Index Types
articles.author: The PostgreSQL Global Development Group
articles.text:
PostgreSQL offers several index types: B-tree, Hash, GiST, SP-GiST, GIN, and BRIN.

The B-tree index is the default and handles equality and range queries on sortable data. GIN indexes values that contain many elements, such as arrays and full-text search documents, and BRIN keeps a tiny summary of block ranges for very large tables whose order follows a column. The query planner chooses whether an index helps a given query.

articles.title: Routine Vacuuming
articles.author: The PostgreSQL Global Development Group
articles.text:
Because of MVCC, PostgreSQL must vacuum its tables regularly.

Vacuum reclaims the space of dead tuples left by updates and deletes, updates the statistics used by the query planner, keeps the visibility map current for index-only scans, and protects against transaction ID wraparound. The autovacuum daemon does this automatically, and its settings can be tuned for tables with heavy write traffic.

articles.title: Write-Ahead Logging
articles.author: The PostgreSQL Global Development Group
articles.text:
Write-ahead logging is the standard way to ensure data integrity: changes are written to the write-ahead log before the data files.

After a crash, PostgreSQL replays the write-ahead log to recover. The log is written sequentially, so a commit costs one flush of the log instead of flushes of every changed data page. The same write-ahead log enables point-in-time recovery and streaming replication to standby servers.

articles.title: Log-Shipping Standby Servers
articles.author: The PostgreSQL Global Development Group
articles.text:
PostgreSQL keeps standby servers in step with a primary by shipping its write-ahead log.

With streaming replication, the standby receives the write-ahead log as it is generated and can serve read-only queries as a hot standby. Replication is asynchronous by default; synchronous replication waits for a standby to confirm each commit, trading latency for durability. If the primary fails, a standby can be promoted, but PostgreSQL itself does not decide when: that needs a failover manager, often built on a consensus store.

articles.title: Pod Security Standards
articles.author: Kubernetes
articles.text:
Kubernetes defines three policies for pods: Privileged, unrestricted; Baseline, which blocks the known privilege escalations; and Restricted, which follows current hardening practice.

A cluster applies them per namespace with the built-in Pod Security admission controller, to enforce, audit, or only warn. Restricted asks containers to run as non-root, drop capabilities, and use a seccomp profile, which limits what an attacker can do from a compromised container.

articles.title: StatefulSets
articles.author: Kubernetes
articles.text:
A StatefulSet runs pods that need a stable identity and stable storage, such as databases.

Each pod gets a persistent name and its own persistent volume, which follows it when it is rescheduled, and pods are created, scaled, and updated in order. Running a database such as PostgreSQL on a Kubernetes cluster usually starts with a StatefulSet, with an operator on top to handle replication, backups, and failover.

articles.title: Operator pattern
articles.author: Kubernetes
articles.text:
An operator extends Kubernetes with custom resources and a controller that encodes the knowledge of a human operator.

The controller watches the cluster and reconciles the actual state toward the desired state, the same control loop that Kubernetes uses for its own objects. Operators automate tasks such as deploying a database cluster, taking backups, handling upgrades, and recovering from failures.

articles.title: etcd: a distributed, reliable key-value store
articles.author: etcd
articles.text:
etcd is a strongly consistent, distributed key-value store for the critical data of a distributed system, and it holds the whole state of a Kubernetes cluster.

It uses the Raft consensus algorithm to replicate its log across a cluster of members: a leader is elected, and a write is committed once a quorum of members has stored it. etcd keeps working as long as a majority of its members is available, and clients can watch keys to react to changes.

articles.title: Secrets
articles.author: Kubernetes
articles.text:
A Secret holds a small amount of sensitive data, such as a password or a token, so it does not have to be put in a container image or a pod specification.

By default, Secrets are stored unencrypted in etcd, base64 encoded only. A cluster should enable encryption at rest, restrict access control to Secrets with RBAC, and limit which containers can read them, because anyone allowed to create a pod in a namespace can read the Secrets of that namespace.

articles.title: What is OpenTelemetry?
articles.author: OpenTelemetry
articles.text:
OpenTelemetry is an observability framework and toolkit to create and manage telemetry data: traces, metrics, and logs.

It is vendor neutral and open source: applications are instrumented once, and the collector sends the data to the observability backend of choice. It is a project of the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, like Kubernetes, and it gives microservices a common way to propagate trace context across service boundaries.

articles.title: Fixing For Loops in Go 1.22
articles.author: Russ Cox
articles.text:
Go 1.22 gives each iteration of a for loop its own copy of the loop variable, so closures and goroutines started in the loop no longer share one variable by accident.

The old behaviour caused real bugs: a goroutine or a closure captured the loop variable and saw its last value instead of the value of its own iteration. Go 1.21 offers a preview behind GOEXPERIMENT=loopvar, and the change only applies to modules that declare Go 1.22 or later in their go.mod, so old code keeps its meaning. The Go toolchain ships a tool to find the loops whose behaviour changes.

articles.title: The Raft Consensus Algorithm
articles.author: Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout
articles.text:
Raft is a consensus algorithm designed to be easy to understand, and equivalent to Paxos in fault tolerance and performance.

It separates leader election, log replication, and safety. A leader is elected for a term, it appends commands to its log and replicates them to the followers, and an entry is committed once a quorum of servers has it. A cluster of servers can thus agree on a replicated log even when some of them fail. etcd, Consul, and many databases use Raft.

articles.title: OWASP Top Ten
articles.author: OWASP Foundation
articles.text:
The OWASP Top 10 is the standard awareness document on the most critical security risks of web applications, built from data and a community survey.

Broken access control leads the 2021 edition, followed by cryptographic failures and injection, which includes SQL injection. Insecure design, security misconfiguration, and vulnerable and outdated components, a software supply chain risk, follow. Each risk comes with ways to prevent it.

articles.title: Appropriate Uses For SQLite
articles.author: SQLite
articles.text:
SQLite does not compete with client/server databases; it competes with fopen().

The page lists where an embedded database shines, from devices and application file formats to websites with modest traffic and data analysis, and where a client/server database such as PostgreSQL is the better choice: data spread over a network, very high write concurrency, or very large datasets.

articles.title: Microservices
articles.author: James Lewis and Martin Fowler
articles.text:
The article that named the microservices style: an application built as a suite of small services, each running in its own process, deployed independently, and organised around business capabilities.

It weighs smart endpoints and dumb pipes, decentralised data management, where each service owns its database, and infrastructure automation, against the cost of a distributed system: network failures, eventual consistency between services, and harder operations.

articles.title: Consistency Models
articles.author: Jepsen
articles.text:
A map of consistency models for databases and distributed systems, from strict serializability and linearizability down to read committed and eventual consistency.

Each model says which histories of operations a system may show, and the map shows which models imply which. It also shows which models stay available during a network partition and which need a quorum or a leader, which is the practical side of the CAP theorem.

articles.title: How to do distributed locking
articles.author: Martin Kleppmann
articles.text:
A distributed lock is either for efficiency, to avoid doing work twice, or for correctness, to keep data safe.

For correctness, a lock with a lease is not enough: a process can pause for garbage collection or lose the network, its lease expires, and another process takes the lock while the first still believes it holds it. The fix is a fencing token, a number that grows with each grant and that the storage checks. The article argues that Redlock depends on timing assumptions, and that correctness needs a consensus system such as ZooKeeper or etcd.

articles.title: Concurrency is not Parallelism by Rob Pike
articles.author: Rob Pike
articles.text: Rob Pike's talk at Heroku's Waza conference in 2012: concurrency is the composition of independently executing processes, parallelism is their simultaneous execution, and Go's goroutines and channels are tools for the first. Slides: https://talks.golang.org/2012/waza.slide

articles.title: Managing Critical State: Distributed Consensus for Reliability
articles.author: Laura Nolan, Site Reliability Engineering
articles.text:
A chapter of Google's Site Reliability Engineering book on distributed consensus.

Leader election, critical shared state, and distributed locking all need consensus, and ad hoc solutions break during a network partition. The chapter explains how Paxos and Raft reach agreement with a quorum, and how to deploy them: the number of replicas, their placement across failure domains, and the latency cost of each round trip.

articles.title: Eventually Consistent - Revisited
articles.author: Werner Vogels
articles.text:
Amazon's CTO explains the trade-offs behind eventual consistency in large distributed systems.

With replication across many servers and data centres, a system cannot have strong consistency and stay available during a network partition. Eventual consistency promises that, without new updates, all replicas converge. The article describes the variants that make it usable, such as read-your-writes and monotonic reads, and how quorum sizes for reads and writes set the balance.

articles.title: SLSA: Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts
articles.author: OpenSSF
articles.text:
SLSA is a security framework to protect the software supply chain, from source to build to package.

Its levels describe increasing guarantees about how an artifact was built: provenance that says what was built, from which source, and by which build system, then builds on a hardened platform that a tenant cannot tamper with. Consumers verify the provenance before they deploy, which stops tampered artifacts and many supply chain attacks.

articles.title: Secure by Design
articles.author: CISA
articles.text:
Secure by design asks software manufacturers to take ownership of the security outcomes of their customers.

Products should be secure out of the box: multi-factor authentication by default, no default passwords, memory-safe languages for new code, and the elimination of whole classes of vulnerability such as SQL injection, rather than patching them one by one. Manufacturers should be transparent about vulnerabilities and lead from the top.

articles.title: SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet
articles.author: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series
articles.text:
SQL injection happens when user input is concatenated into a SQL query, so an attacker can change the query.

The primary defence is prepared statements with parameterized queries, where the database receives the query and its parameters separately. Stored procedures written safely, and allow-list input validation for the parts of a query that cannot be parameters, such as table names, come next. Least privilege for the database account limits the damage when an injection gets through.

articles.title: OWASP Application Security Verification Standard
articles.author: OWASP Foundation
articles.text:
The ASVS is a list of security requirements to design, build, and test web applications and services.

Its three levels go from the minimum every application should meet to the depth expected of critical applications. Requirements cover authentication, session management, access control, validation and encoding against injection, cryptography, and configuration, and each one can be verified, which makes the standard useful for architecture, code review, and penetration testing.

articles.title: Use The Index, Luke!
articles.author: Markus Winand
articles.text:
A guide to SQL indexing and performance for developers.

It explains how a B-tree index works, why the order of columns in an index matters, how the query planner decides to use an index, and how to read an execution plan. It covers PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, and SQL Server, and argues that indexing is a development task, because only developers know how the application queries its data.

articles.title: "Raft - The Understandable Distributed Protocol" by Ben Johnson (2013)
articles.author: Strange Loop Conference
articles.text:
For the last decade, Paxos has been the de facto standard in distributed protocols. Unfortunately, Paxos is difficult to understand and even harder to implement. The implementors of Google's distributed lock system called "Chubby" even stated that there were many gaps in Paxos when it came to real world implementation.

Recently a new distributed protocol has come out of research at Stanford called Raft. Raft is built for real world applications and a primary concern in the development of the protocol was understandability. This talk will walk you through the Raft protocol and how it works.

articles.title: "The Mess We're In" by Joe Armstrong
articles.author: Strange Loop Conference
articles.text: Joe Armstrong is one of the inventors of Erlang. When at the Ericsson computer science lab in 1986, he was part of the team who designed and implemented the first version of Erlang. He has written several Erlang books including Programming Erlang Software for a Concurrent World. Joe has a PhD in computer science from the Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm, Sweden.

articles.title: "Simple Made Easy" - Rich Hickey (2011)
articles.author: Strange Loop Conference
articles.text:
Rich Hickey, the author of Clojure and designer of Datomic, is a software developer with over 30 years of experience in various domains. Rich has worked on scheduling systems, broadcast automation, audio analysis and fingerprinting, database design, yield management, exit poll systems, and machine listening, in a variety of languages.

This keynote was given at Strange Loop 2011, and is perhaps the best known and most highly regarded of Rich's many excellent talks, ushering in a new way to think about the problems of software design and the constant fight against complexity.

articles.title: Gopherfest 2015 | Go Proverbs with Rob Pike
articles.author: The Go Programming Language
articles.text: Rob Pike's talk at Gopherfest 2015 on the Go proverbs: short sayings that capture how to write Go, such as "don't communicate by sharing memory, share memory by communicating" and "a little copying is better than a little dependency".
